subsections.subsection_title: 33. COUNSELLING A MOTHER OF A PRETERM BABY

blocks.text: This is a likely communication station.
“I understand that having your baby arrive earlier than expected can be frightening. The neonatal team will monitor the baby closely and support the baby while the organs continue to mature.”
Explain:

“Premature babies can have difficulty maintaining their temperature, breathing independently, feeding and maintaining their blood sugar. They are also more vulnerable to infections and certain complications.”
Then reassure without giving false promises:
“The exact problems depend on how premature the baby is and how the baby is doing clinically.”

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What is the difference between prematurity and LBW?

blocks.text: “Prematurity is defined by gestational age, whereas low birth weight is defined by birth weight.”

content_groups.group_title: Q6. List five complications of prematurity.

blocks.text: A good answer:
“Respiratory distress syndrome, apnoea, intraventricular haemorrhage, necrotising enterocolitis and retinopathy of prematurity.”
Then add:
“Other complications include hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, sepsis, PDA, jaundice, anaemia and long-term neurodevelopmental problems.”

content_groups.group_title: Q7. Why does a premature infant develop respiratory distress syndrome?

blocks.text: “Because of inadequate pulmonary surfactant production resulting from immature type II pneumocytes.”

content_groups.group_title: Q8. Why are premature babies prone to hypothermia?

blocks.text: “They have a large surface-area-to-volume ratio, thin skin, little subcutaneous fat and immature thermoregulation.”

content_groups.group_title: Q9. Why are they prone to hypoglycaemia?

blocks.text: “They have limited glycogen and fat stores, immature metabolic adaptation and relatively high metabolic requirements.”

content_groups.group_title: Q10. Why are they prone to NEC?

blocks.text: “The immature intestine has impaired barrier and immune function and abnormal intestinal perfusion and motility, increasing susceptibility to intestinal injury and inflammation.”

content_groups.group_title: Q11. What is the major eye complication of prematurity?

blocks.text: “Retinopathy of prematurity.”

content_groups.group_title: Q12. What is the neurological complication you should remember?

blocks.text: “Intraventricular haemorrhage in very preterm infants, with possible later neurodevelopmental impairment.”

content_groups.group_title: Q13. What is the preferred milk for a preterm infant?

blocks.text: “Mother's own breast milk whenever possible.”

content_groups.group_title: Q14. What is kangaroo mother care?

blocks.text: “Skin-to-skin care of the newborn with the mother or another appropriate caregiver, combined with appropriate feeding and follow-up.”
A baby is born at **29 weeks**, weighing **1.2 kg**.
“What is your assessment?”
“This is an extremely vulnerable very preterm infant with very low birth weight who is showing signs of respiratory distress, most likely requiring assessment for respiratory distress syndrome.”
“What will you do?”

“I would assess airway, breathing and circulation immediately, monitor oxygen saturation and cardiorespiratory status, maintain thermal stability, obtain appropriate investigations including blood gas where indicated, and provide respiratory support according to severity and neonatal protocol. I would consider CPAP and surfactant therapy where indicated.”
Then:
“I would also monitor glucose, fluid balance and feeding, and assess for sepsis and other complications of prematurity.”
A **30-week infant** develops abdominal distension, bloody stool and feeding intolerance.

Answer:
**Necrotising** **enterocolitis.**

“I would stop enteral feeds, commence appropriate gastric decompression, provide intravenous fluids and nutritional support, obtain appropriate investigations including abdominal imaging and blood tests, assess for sepsis and perforation, and commence antibiotics according to the local neonatal protocol. I would involve the neonatal and paediatric surgical teams if there is concern for perforation or severe disease.”

But for exams, the simpler list is often better:

If asked:
**“Summarise the management of a premature infant.”**
Say:

“Management is multidisciplinary and begins with maintaining airway, breathing and circulation, preventing hypothermia, monitoring and treating hypoglycaemia, providing appropriate respiratory support, ensuring adequate nutrition preferably with mother's own breast milk, preventing and treating infection, monitoring for complications such as NEC, IVH, PDA and ROP, and providing developmental care and appropriate follow-up.”
The easiest way to structure almost any premature-baby OSCE is:
**HOW PREMATURE? → HOW SMALL? → HOW SICK? → WHAT COMPLICATIONS? → SUPPORT THE ORGANS → FEED → PREVENT COMPLICATIONS → FOLLOW UP**
That structure prevents you from missing the major areas.
